title: The Economics of Ecosystems and Biodiversity
article: The Economics of Ecosystems and Biodiversity

definition.text: TEEB was an international study, led by Pavan Sukhdev from 2007 to 2011, that set out to show the global economic benefits of biodiversity and the rising cost of losing it.

facts.text: Germany and the European Commission launched TEEB in 2007, answering a proposal by G8+5 environment ministers meeting in Potsdam for a global study of the economics of biodiversity loss.
Its 2008 interim report focused largely on forests and put the loss of natural capital from deforestation and degradation at US$2–4.5 trillion per year.
It estimated that investing US$45 billion a year in protected areas alone could secure ecosystem services worth some US$5 trillion a year.
Phase II was presented in October 2010 at the 10th Conference of the Parties of the Convention on Biological Diversity in Nagoya, Japan.
A central aim was an economic yardstick better than GDP, and national accounts broad enough to measure the welfare benefits ecosystems provide.
TEEB reported that ecosystem service values run from about $100 per hectare per year for open ocean to over $1,000,000 per hectare per year for the richest coral reefs.
Critics argue that basing nature's value on human preferences cannot tell us what is ecologically essential to keep life-support systems working.

contested_note: Critics dispute whether valuing ecosystems by human preferences, as TEEB does, can guide what nature must be protected.

title: Stockholm Conference of 1972
article: United Nations Conference on the Human Environment

definition.text: The United Nations Conference on the Human Environment, held in Stockholm from 5 to 16 June 1972, was the first global conference on environmental issues.

facts.text: Sweden proposed the idea to the UN Economic and Social Council in 1968, and preparations took four years, involved 114 governments and cost over $30,000,000.
The conference created the United Nations Environment Programme (UNEP), the first UN agency headquartered in a developing country, in Nairobi.
It agreed a Declaration of 26 principles on environment and development, an Action Plan of 109 recommendations, and a Resolution.
Divisions between rich and poor countries surfaced; developing countries made up 70 of the 122 countries attending, while the Soviet bloc boycotted it.
Indira Gandhi's speech linked ecological management with relieving poverty, which became one of the conference's central themes.
It spurred countries to monitor their environments and set up environment ministries and agencies.
The 1992 Rio Earth Summit, the 2002 Johannesburg summit and Rio+20 in 2012 all took the Stockholm declaration as their starting point.

sources.title: United Nations Conference on the Human Environment
sources.key: United Nations Conference on the Human Environment

definition.text: The Earth Summit was the United Nations Conference on Environment and Development, held in Rio de Janeiro from 3 to 14 June 1992.

facts.text: It was attended by 108 heads of state and government and helped establish and spread the idea of sustainable development.
A key achievement was the UN Framework Convention on Climate Change, signed by 154 states, which later led to the Kyoto Protocol and the Paris Agreement.
The Convention on Biological Diversity was opened for signature at the summit.
It produced the Rio Declaration and Agenda 21, which 178 governments voted to adopt, and set up the Commission on Sustainable Development to oversee them.
It helped spread key treaty principles: the precautionary principle, common but differentiated responsibilities, and the polluter pays principle.
Critics note that many Rio agreements, on fighting poverty and cleaning up the environment, were never realized, and some leaders called it green imperialism by the global North.

definition.text: Our Common Future, or the Brundtland Report, is the 1987 report of the UN's World Commission on Environment and Development that set out the best-known definition of sustainable development.

facts.text: It defined sustainable development as development that meets present needs without compromising the ability of future generations to meet their own needs.
It treated environment and development as one single issue and stressed the interlocking economic, environmental and social sides of human development.
It held that poverty worsens environmental pressure, and recognized that environmental limits to economic growth exist.
The report came out of a 900-day worldwide exercise of public hearings and expert testimony, chaired by former Norwegian Prime Minister Gro Harlem Brundtland.
It laid the groundwork for the 1992 Earth Summit, Agenda 21 and the Rio Declaration.
In 1988 Helge Ole Bergesen wrote that Third World elites saw the report as green imperialism.

definition.text: A Sand County Almanac is a 1949 book of essays by the American ecologist and forester Aldo Leopold that argues for a 'land ethic', a responsible relationship between people and the land.

facts.text: Leopold's land ethic holds that a thing is right when it tends to preserve the integrity, stability and beauty of the biotic community, and wrong when it does not.
Leopold argued that land is not a commodity to be owned, and objected that policy makers always need an economic motive before they will conserve.
The essay 'Thinking Like a Mountain' describes, in plain words, how killing top predators such as wolves ripples through the rest of the ecosystem.
Little noticed at first, it became a surprise bestseller in the 1970s; over two million copies have been printed.
A 1990 poll of the American Nature Study Society ranked it with Silent Spring as the two most significant environmental books of the 20th century.

title: Silent Spring

definition.text: Silent Spring is Rachel Carson's 1962 environmental science book documenting the harm done by indiscriminate use of the pesticide DDT.

facts.text: Carson argued that pesticides harm the wider environment and should be called 'biocides', because their effects rarely stop at the target pests.
She accused the chemical industry of spreading disinformation and officials of accepting its claims without question.

Despite fierce opposition from chemical companies, it shifted public opinion, reversed US pesticide policy, led to a national ban on DDT for farm use, and fed the movement that created the US Environmental Protection Agency.
It became a rallying point for the new social movement of the 1960s and is seen as the beginning of the contemporary deep ecology movement.
One scholar said that after it, no one could sell pollution as the necessary underside of progress so easily.
Some anti-environmentalist groups blame Carson for malaria deaths after DDT restrictions; scientists and journalists have dismissed this claim as a myth.

contested_note: Opponents of DDT restrictions blame the book for malaria deaths, while other scientists call that claim a myth.

title: Rio+20
article: United Nations Conference on Sustainable Development

definition.text: Rio+20, the United Nations Conference on Sustainable Development, was a 2012 summit in Rio de Janeiro that sought to reconcile the world's economic and environmental goals.

facts.text: Held from 13 to 22 June 2012, it marked 20 years since the 1992 Earth Summit in the same city.
Its two main themes were building a green economy that lifts people out of poverty, and an institutional framework for sustainable development.
Its 49-page nonbinding outcome document, 'The Future We Want', called for the Sustainable Development Goals, a set of measurable targets.
Nations agreed to explore alternatives to GDP that count environmental and social factors, such as nature's carbon storage and habitat protection.
All nations reaffirmed commitments to phase out fossil fuel subsidies.
It popularised the term blue economy and saw the launch of the Inclusive Wealth Report.
Leaders such as Obama, Merkel and Cameron stayed away, which was read as a sign that sustainability was not their priority.

definition.text: The World Summit on Sustainable Development, nicknamed Rio+10, was held in Johannesburg, South Africa, from 26 August to 4 September 2002.

facts.text: There, sustainable development was recognized as an overarching goal for national, regional and international institutions.
Instead of new treaties it produced almost 300 'partnership initiatives' meant to help reach the Millennium Development Goals, plus the Johannesburg Declaration.
US President George W. Bush boycotted the summit, which left it partly impotent.

title: MONDIACULT
article: World Conference on Cultural Policies and Sustainable Development

definition.text: MONDIACULT, the World Conference on Cultural Policies and Sustainable Development, is a series of UNESCO conferences at which member states set the global agenda for culture.

facts.text: First held in Mexico City in 1982, it affirmed culture as a fundamental dimension of development.
Relaunched in 2022, it recognized culture as a global public good and called for its inclusion in the post-2030 sustainable development agenda.

title: An Essay on the Principle of Population
article: An Essay on the Principle of Population

definition.text: An Essay on the Principle of Population is Thomas Robert Malthus's 1798 book arguing that population tends to grow until it outruns the supply of food and other basic resources.

facts.text: Malthus argued that population expands in times of plenty until it becomes too large for the more modest supply of primary resources, causing distress.
He named two checks that hold population within resource limits: preventive checks that lower births, such as delayed marriage, and positive checks that raise deaths, such as hunger, disease and war.
He linked population to wages: when workers multiply faster than food output, food costs rise and real wages fall, which in turn slows population growth.
Darwin and Wallace both credited Malthus with helping them develop the theory of natural selection.
Critics such as Julian Simon note that huge 20th-century population growth did not bring a Malthusian catastrophe, thanks to better farming, machinery, high-yield crops and pesticides.
Later works such as The Population Bomb and The Limits to Growth have been called Malthusian.

contested_note: Whether Malthus's limits on population hold is disputed: critics point out that food output kept pace with 20th-century population growth.

definition.text: Classical economics is the school of economic thought that flourished mainly in Britain from the late 18th to the mid-19th century, led by Adam Smith, David Ricardo, Thomas Malthus and John Stuart Mill.

facts.text: Adam Smith's The Wealth of Nations of 1776 is usually taken to mark its beginning.
The classical economists saw markets as largely self-regulating systems, a view captured by Smith's metaphor of the invisible hand.
Smith held that a nation's wealth is its yearly income, produced by labour, land and capital and shared out as wages, rent and profits.
They favoured free trade over the protectionism of the earlier mercantilists, and Ricardo explained trade's gains through comparative advantage.
John Stuart Mill believed a future 'stationary state' with constant population and capital was inevitable and desirable, an idea now called a steady-state economy.
From the 1870s it gave way to neoclassical economics, though many of its ideas remain fundamental.
Thomas Carlyle nicknamed it 'the dismal science', a jibe often linked to Malthus's gloomy analysis.

title: Classical theory of value

definition.text: The classical theory of value explained prices by a 'natural price' set by lasting forces, toward which day-to-day market prices tend to move.

facts.text: William Petty first separated the market price, pushed about by passing influences, from the natural price.
Smith said market prices are drawn toward natural prices, somewhat like gravity.
For Smith the natural price was the sum of the natural rates of wages, profits and rent.
Petty held a land-and-labour theory of value, while the labour theory of value later clashed with Ricardo's comparative advantage.

contested_note: The theory of value, and how classical economics relates to neoclassical economics, are still debated.

definition.text: The conservation movement is an environmental, social and political movement that seeks to manage and protect natural resources, wild species and their habitats for the future.

facts.text: It grew from the practical need to keep up fisheries, wildlife, water, soil and forests.
It is often traced to John Evelyn's Sylva of 1662, which urged England to manage the rate of tree felling and replant cut trees.
Its 19th-century ethic held that human activity harms the environment, that there is a civic duty to keep it for future generations, and that science should guide that duty.
The first practical use of scientific conservation was in the forests of India in the mid-19th century.
It has broadened from sustainable yields of resources and wilderness preservation to the preservation of biodiversity.
Scholars note that early conservation often protected game for elite white hunters while policing hunting by Indigenous and poor people.

title: Stockholm Declaration
article: Declaration of the United Nations Conference on the Human Environment

definition.text: The Stockholm Declaration of 1972 was the first United Nations declaration on the global environment, a set of 26 principles agreed at the Stockholm Conference.

facts.text: Its first principle says people have a right to an environment of a quality that allows a life of dignity and well-being, and a duty to protect it for present and future generations.
It says Earth's capacity to produce vital renewable resources must be maintained and, where practicable, restored.
Principle 21, its legal core, gives states sovereign rights over their own territory along with a responsibility not to harm others across borders.
Developing countries argued that rich nations used most resources and caused most pollution, so the Global North should bear most of the responsibility.
Indira Gandhi's line that 'poverty is the worst form of pollution' framed a North–South divide that lasted for decades.
It is not legally binding; it counts as soft law, and critics called much of it too vague for legal use.
It shaped later treaties, and the 1992 Rio Declaration adopted a modified Principle 21.

definition.text: Earth Day is an annual event held on April 22 to show support for environmental protection, first held in 1970.

facts.text: US Senator Gaylord Nelson proposed a nationwide environmental teach-in for April 22, 1970, and hired the young activist Denis Hayes to coordinate it.
Nelson was moved to act after the 1969 Santa Barbara oil spill, which released over 3 million US gallons of oil and killed more than 10,000 seabirds and sea mammals.
The 1970s that followed brought major US environmental laws such as the Clean Air Act and Clean Water Act, the creation of the EPA, and bans on DDT and leaded gasoline.
In 1990 it went global, mobilizing 200 million people in 141 countries and helping pave the way for the 1992 Earth Summit.
The Paris Agreement was signed on Earth Day 2016 by leaders of 175 nations.
Nelson summed up the movement's view: 'The economy is a wholly owned subsidiary of the environment, not the other way around.'

definition.text: Physiocracy, from the Greek for 'government of nature', was an 18th-century French economic theory holding that a nation's wealth comes solely from its land and farming.

facts.text: It was one of the first well-developed theories of economics, led by François Quesnay, the Marquis de Mirabeau and Turgot, just before Adam Smith's classical economics.
The physiocrats saw productive work as the source of national wealth, unlike the mercantilists who focused on the ruler's gold or the balance of trade.
Only farm labour created value in their view; industry and other work were 'unproductive appendages' to agriculture.
They believed in a 'natural order' and in laissez-faire, the idea that self-interest and free trade, not state restriction, make the economy work.
Turgot was among the first to see diminishing returns: adding more of an input raises output at a falling rate, so wealth cannot grow without limit.
Their ideas influenced Smith, Ricardo and Mill, and Henry George's proposal to fund government by taxing land values.

definition.text: The Tableau économique is an economic model François Quesnay described in 1759 that traced how production and money flow between social classes.

facts.text: It had three classes: landowners, farm workers as the 'productive' class, and artisans and merchants as the 'sterile' class.
Quesnay, a physician, likened the circulation of wealth to the circulation of blood in the body.
It holds the origins of modern ideas about the circulation of wealth and how the parts of an economy depend on one another.

definition.text: Small Is Beautiful: A Study of Economics As If People Mattered is a 1973 essay collection by the economist E. F. Schumacher that criticizes mainstream economics for ignoring nature's limits.

facts.text: Schumacher argued that the modern economy is unsustainable because it treats natural resources such as fossil fuels as spendable income rather than as capital that will run out.
He added that nature's ability to absorb pollution is also limited.
His philosophy of 'enoughness' grew from his study of village economies, which he called Buddhist economics.
The title came from his teacher Leopold Kohr's case for small, appropriate technologies over 'bigger is better'; the book inspired the appropriate technology movement.
The 1973 energy crisis helped it reach a wide audience, and in 1995 it was ranked among the 100 most influential books since World War II.

title: The Population Bomb

definition.text: The Population Bomb is a 1968 book by Paul and Anne Ehrlich that predicted worldwide famines from overpopulation and called for immediate limits on population growth.

facts.text: Its opening claimed that in the 1970s hundreds of millions would starve to death whatever was done.
Critics call it a restatement of Malthus's argument that population will outgrow farm output unless controlled.
Instead, the global death rate kept falling, from 13 per 1000 in 1965–74 to 10 per 1000 in 1985–90, while calories per person rose 24%.
Julian Simon and Hans Rosling argued its forecasts wrongly assumed exponential growth would continue with no technological or social progress.
Barry Commoner argued that helping poor people grow richer would lower birth rates on its own, making coercive population policies unnecessary.
The Ehrlichs stand by its core claim that population growth is a major problem and say it brought human numbers into environmental debate.

contested_note: Critics say its famine predictions failed and its thesis was wrong, while the authors and some supporters hold its core warning was prescient.

definition.text: The history of economic thought is the study of the thinkers and theories behind political economy and economics, from the ancient world to today.

facts.text: In the West, economics was part of philosophy rather than a separate discipline until the Industrial Revolution of the 18th and 19th centuries.
Mercantilism dominated Europe from the 16th to the 18th century, until the physiocrats and then Adam Smith's classical economics challenged it.
Neoclassical economics developed in the 1870s in three independent schools: the Cambridge, Austrian and Lausanne schools.
In 1920 Arthur Cecil Pigou argued that markets fail when there are externalities, so the state must step in.
In the 1930s economists began modelling how to manage non-renewable resources and whether welfare can be sustained in an economy that uses them up.
Malthus on overpopulation and Mill on the stationary state anticipated the concerns of ecological economics, founded in the work of Boulding, Georgescu-Roegen and Daly.

title: Mercantilism

definition.text: Mercantilism is a nationalist economic policy that aims to maximize a country's exports and minimize its imports.

facts.text: Mercantilists held that money and precious metals were the only true riches, so tariffs should encourage exports and discourage imports.
They believed international trade could not benefit all countries at once.
It dominated modernizing Europe from the 16th to the 19th centuries; Adam Smith vigorously opposed it and argued for free trade.

notes: Mentioned on Physiocracy, Classical economics and History of economic thought; may belong in an economics-basics chapter.

title: The Economics of Welfare

definition.text: The Economics of Welfare is Arthur Cecil Pigou's 1920 book that introduced the idea of the externality and proposed correcting it with a tax.

facts.text: Pigou built on Alfred Marshall's idea of an externality: a cost or benefit falling on others that the person causing it does not account for.
It first planted the idea that governments should tax activities that put uncompensated costs on others, now called a Pigouvian tax.
Pigou applied the reasoning to traffic congestion, an early case of what became congestion pricing.
It argued that markets are inefficient when externalities exist, so the state must intervene.

notes: Phrase concept with no page of its own. One source (163d71c79ad7) dates a later edition 1932; the work was first published as Wealth and Welfare and retitled.

title: Conservation Reconsidered

definition.text: Conservation Reconsidered is John V. Krutilla's 1967 paper describing the economic value of undisturbed natural places such as rivers and forests.

facts.text: In it Krutilla introduced existence value, the value people get from the mere existence of something such as unspoiled wilderness or a species, even if they never use it.
This idea of 'nonuse value' made Krutilla a pioneer of environmental economics.

notes: Phrase concept with no page of its own.

title: Club of Rome

definition.text: An informal non-profit group of intellectuals and business leaders, founded in Rome in 1968, that critically discusses pressing global problems.

facts.text: Italian industrialist Aurelio Peccei and British scientist Alexander King founded it, sharing doubts that development and technological progress could solve the world's problems.

Its first report, The Limits to Growth (1972), used computer simulations suggesting that growth in production and consumption could not continue indefinitely because of resource depletion or pollution.
The report sold 30 million copies in more than 30 languages, making it the best-selling environmental book in history.
Its questioning of growth provoked hostile reactions at the OECD, which set its course on unfettered growth.
Economist Robert Solow called The Limits to Growth scenarios 'simplistic'; a 1973 Sussex University study, Models of Doom, found its forecasts hinged on a few unduly pessimistic assumptions.
In 2009 Solow allowed that rapid growth in India and China might make real demands on natural resources dramatically different.
As of 2025 there had been 55 reports to the club; its Earth4All initiative published 'Earth for All' in 2022, naming five pathways: energy, food, poverty, inequality and population.

contested_note: Critics such as Robert Solow and the Sussex Models of Doom team judged the club's world modelling simplistic and too pessimistic.

title: The Dasgupta Review

definition.text: A 2021 report on the economics of biodiversity, led by economist Partha Dasgupta and commissioned by the UK government.

facts.text: Commissioned by the British Treasury and published in February 2021, it found that biodiversity is declining faster than at any time in human history.
It argued that human demands far exceed nature's capacity to supply the goods and services we rely on, and that current living standards would need 1.6 Earths.
It called for changes akin to or greater than the Marshall Plan, including abandoning GDP as the measure of economic success and social progress.
In June 2021 the UK government committed to a nature-positive future in response to its findings.
The review advocated natural capital thinking; ecological economist Clive Spash published critical deconstructions of it.

notes: No page of its own; mentioned on Partha Dasgupta, Economic growth, Anthropocene, Nature-positive and Clive Spash.
